QuickClinic — Appointment Booking App

In short: a healthcare booking app for iOS and Android that lets patients see real waiting times and confirm a same-day appointment in a few taps — instead of ringing round clinics and hoping someone picks up.

Overview

QuickClinic lets patients book doctor appointments instantly — find specialists, check availability, get reminders, and manage their health in one place. I designed the product end to end, from research through to the final UI: the booking flow, the information architecture, the design system, and the 20+ screens that make up the app.

Role

UX/UI Designer — user research, personas and empathy mapping, information architecture, sketches and wireframes, design system, interactive prototype, usability testing, and final visual design.

Platform — iOS & Android 20+ Hi-Fi Screens

Problem

Patients using healthcare booking apps are left in the dark — unable to see accurate wait times or confirm same-day appointments. That forces them to make uninformed decisions about their care, leading to frustration, wasted time, and in some cases delayed treatment for urgent health needs.

  • No visibility into how long the wait will actually be
  • No way to confirm a same-day slot without phoning
  • Calls to clinics that go unanswered, with no fallback

Solution

A simple booking platform that lets patients confirm a same-day appointment with their own doctor, showing real-time availability and waiting times up front. Patients secure appointments faster and avoid long waits, which makes access to care more predictable and far less stressful.

Design Process

I followed a user-centered process, starting with research into what patients and doctors actually need, then moving into wireframes and prototypes. Iterative testing and feedback shaped the interface until booking an appointment was simple, fast, and reliable.

Idea → Research → UX / Wireframes → Prototyping → User Testing → UI Design → Presentation

User Research

The goal was to pin down where booking actually breaks down for people — what gets in their way, and what they need to know before they'll commit to visiting a clinic. Four findings shaped everything downstream:

  • Location-based. Distance and travel time strongly influence which clinic people choose.
  • Booking confirmation. Users want same-day slots, or confirmation within one to two hours.
  • Clinic barriers. Clinics don't always answer the phone, which creates delay and frustration.
  • Messaging helps. Users want to message a clinic for quick questions, not just call.

Users

Two personas carried the design decisions — one booking for herself around a full working day, one booking for his child.

Sehar, 35

Financial Analyst

Sehar works full-time on a tight schedule and values convenience. She prefers to book digitally, needs same-day appointments, and relies on accurate wait times to plan around work.

Goals

  • Find nearby clinics quickly
  • Book an appointment in a few minutes
  • Avoid long waiting times

Pain

  • Calling multiple clinics to check availability
  • Uncertain waiting times
  • Difficulty fitting appointments into a work schedule

Vincent, 37

Software Engineer

Vincent searches for clinics for his child and needs options he can trust. He prefers clear information about the doctor and the services available before he commits to a booking.

Goals

  • Quickly find pediatric or family clinics
  • Book appointments without delays
  • Reduce waiting time for his child

Pain

  • Hard to find available pediatric doctors
  • Long waiting times at the clinic
  • Lack of clear appointment confirmation

Empathy Mapping

Mapping what each persona thinks, feels, says, and does turned the research notes into something I could design against — and made it obvious that the anxiety sits in the gap between requesting an appointment and having it confirmed.

Information Architecture

I mapped the whole product as a single tree so the booking path stayed short no matter where someone entered it. Home branches into search, categories, scheduled appointments, nearby doctors, recent visits, and featured services — and every one of those routes converges on the same doctor card and booking flow, rather than each having its own variant.

Sketches

Rough sketches let me explore layout options fast and cheaply, and gave me a way to compare several structures for the home and booking screens before committing any of them to a wireframe.

Design System

Satoshi does the typographic work — a clean, modern sans-serif with a simple, versatile range of weights. The palette runs from a deep clinical blue through to a near-white wash, which keeps the interface calm and lets the one accent colour carry every primary action.

#013952 · #5B8998 · #95C3D2 · #CEE3EA · #EBFAFF

Spacing & Grid

A defined grid and consistent spacing hold the interface together across every screen, which is what makes the app feel clean and easy to navigate rather than merely tidy on any one screen.

Hi-Fidelity Wireframes

Twenty-plus screens in near-final form — refined layout, typography, spacing, and visual hierarchy, but still greyscale. Working this way let me settle structure and hierarchy while colour was still off the table, so the transition into final UI was a matter of applying the system rather than re-deciding the layout.

Key Decisions — UX Laws Applied

Four principles did most of the heavy lifting, and each one resolved a specific decision rather than sitting in the deck as decoration.

Hick's Law

Decision time grows with more choices.

  • Limit search filters
  • Highlight the best clinics first
  • Offer quick categories — General, Dental, Pediatrics

Fitt's Law

Key actions should be easy to tap.

  • A large, persistent “Book Appointment” button
  • Filters within easy reach
  • Big tap targets for time slots

Miller's Law

Users can hold only so much information at once.

  • Show wait time as a simple range (15–30 min)
  • Progressive booking steps instead of one long form

Jakob's Law

Users prefer interfaces that work like the ones they know.

  • Standard search bar at the top
  • Map plus list view, like common location apps
  • A simple step-by-step booking flow

Usability Testing

I put the prototype in front of users to check whether the booking path held up under real use, and where the interface still asked too much of them.

92%

Found the interface easy to use and intuitive from the first interaction.

85%

Described the design as clean, minimal and visually clear.

Prototype

An interactive prototype brought the product to life, wiring up the key flows and core interactions so navigation, task completion, and system feedback could all be tested properly. It surfaced usability gaps that static screens hid, and let me refine the interactions before any of it reached final UI.

Key Learnings

This project pushed me to design clear, user-friendly booking flows with simplicity, accessibility, and trust as the constraints. The lasting lesson was to reduce friction and handle the edge cases — the unanswered call, the appointment that needs rescheduling — and to think past the visuals to how the product holds up in a real healthcare moment.
